subject: physics
title: Wave-particle duality and electron diffraction
key_idea: Radiation can behave as particles and particles can behave as waves. Electrons fired through graphite diffract, which only waves do. The wavelength of a particle is λ = h/p.

blocks.text: Some experiments show waves and some show particles. Both kinds of behaviour are needed to describe light and matter.

rows: Electromagnetic radiation behaves as a wave
Particles such as electrons behave as waves

items.meaning: The idea that radiation and matter show both wave and particle behaviour.

items: Light shows wave and particle behaviour.
Electrons show wave behaviour as well as particle behaviour.

blocks.text: Fast electrons in a vacuum tube pass through a thin slice of polycrystalline graphite. They hit a fluorescent screen.

items: The graphite atoms are regularly spaced, so they act like a diffraction grating for the electrons.
The screen shows a pattern of concentric rings around a central spot.
Rings are produced by waves that diffract at the atoms and interfere. A stream of simple particles would give a single central spot.
This is evidence for the wave nature of electrons.
Bright rings are where the electron waves interfere constructively.
Many tiny crystals point in random directions, which turns spots into full rings.
The spacing of the atoms is about the same size as the electron wavelength. That is why diffraction occurs.
Electrons diffracted by graphite make a ring pattern.
Diffraction is a wave property, so electrons behave as waves.

blocks.text: A moving particle has an associated wavelength, called the de Broglie wavelength. It depends on the particle's momentum.

items: A bigger momentum gives a shorter wavelength.
Everyday objects have huge momentum, so their wavelength is far too small to notice.
Electrons have tiny mass, so their wavelength is similar to atomic spacing.

diagram.alt: A practice calculation. Given the speed of an electron, find its de Broglie wavelength in nanometres.
diagram.question: An electron travels at {v} × 10⁶ m/s. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength in nm. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, electron mass = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)

blocks.text: Changing the momentum changes the diffraction pattern.

items: Faster electrons have more momentum and a shorter wavelength. The rings become smaller and closer to the centre.
Slower electrons have a longer wavelength. The rings spread out and are wider.
Diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is comparable to the gap spacing.
λ = h/p: more momentum means a shorter wavelength.
More momentum gives less diffraction: the rings shrink.

checks.q: Describe what is seen when electrons pass through thin graphite onto a fluorescent screen, and state what it shows.
checks.a: A pattern of concentric rings appears around a central spot. This shows that electrons diffract, so they behave as waves.

checks.q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron with momentum 1.2 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
The accelerating voltage on the electrons increases. State and explain the effect on the diffraction rings.
checks.a: The electrons gain more momentum, so their wavelength falls. The rings get smaller (closer to the centre).

blocks.text: Our understanding of the nature of matter has changed over time.

items: Particles were first thought to be purely particles, and radiation purely waves.
New evidence, such as electron diffraction, led to a new model.
Such changes are checked by peer review and must be validated by the scientific community before they are accepted.
Details of particular methods of particle diffraction are not required.
Scientific models change when new evidence appears.
Peer review and the scientific community validate the change.

blocks.text: In graphite, the diffraction is caused by the spacing between the atoms, which act as a grating.

items: Two different spacings in the graphite crystal give two rings.
A larger electron wavelength gives larger angles of diffraction.
The pattern is evidence of wave-like behaviour of particles.
Electrons diffract at the atoms of graphite and the spaces between them.
A longer wavelength gives a larger angle of diffraction.
